issues.legal_issue: A tenancy is for manufacturing purposes only when making or fabricating articles is its exclusive or dominant purpose, and repairing or reconditioning goods for storage and resale does not make it a manufacturing tenancy when any manufacture is merely incidental.
material_facts: The tenancy relationship was accepted, but the unregistered lease document could not be used to prove its terms or duration.
The premises contained vehicles acquired for resale, together with spare parts and workshop equipment, and were used to store, repair, recondition and prepare the vehicles for resale.
The evidence that vehicle parts such as chassis and bodies were actually manufactured and substituted was limited to one witness’s bare testimony; no books, logs or other documents supported it.
Even accepting that some spare parts were manufactured, that work was incidental to the principal activity of storing and disposing of the vehicles.
The tenant challenged a possession decree on the ground that a one-month termination notice was insufficient for a manufacturing tenancy.
issues.conclusion: The tenant failed to prove that the exclusive or dominant purpose of the tenancy was manufacturing. The one-month notice was therefore not invalid on the asserted manufacturing-tenancy ground, and the appeal was dismissed. The Court did not decide whether the provision governing the form of leases affected the provision governing the notice period.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, the party asserting a manufacturing tenancy bears the burden of proving that manufacturing was the exclusive or dominant purpose of the lease; C. Mackertich v. Sturt & Co. Ltd., AIR 1970 SC 889, is relied on for that burden. “Manufacture” bears its ordinary meaning: making or fabricating an article, with more than a mere change or repair; a transformation must produce a different article with a distinctive name, character or use. The Court relies on R. v. Wheeler, 2 B. & Ald. 349, South Bihar Sugar Mills v. Union of India, [1968] 3 SCR 21, and Union of India v. Delhi Cloth & General Mills, [1963] Supp. 1 SCR 586, for that meaning. Where the asserted manufacturing purpose is not established, the claimed protection against termination by a one-month notice does not apply.

predicates.possession_decree_appeal: A tenant appealed a decree for possession and relied on the claimed manufacturing purpose of the tenancy to challenge the termination notice.
predicates.premises_used_for_vehicle_storage_and_re: The tenant used the premises to store vehicles and prepare them for resale.
predicates.manufacturing_work_only_incidental: Any making of parts on the premises was subordinate to the main activity of preparing stored goods for disposal.
predicates.manufacturing_purpose_unproven: The tenant did not provide sufficient evidence to establish that making or fabricating articles was the exclusive or dominant purpose of the tenancy.

issues.definition: When a tenant appealing a possession decree used the premises principally to store and resell vehicles, and manufacturing was either incidental or not proved to be the dominant purpose, the notice is valid and the possession decree is upheld.
